title: The afternoon slump
hookLine: a breath practice for the heavy hour
tomorrow: an old hymn, sung as the lamps were lit. what did it praise?

cards: Three in the afternoon. The screen blurs, the clock seems stuck, and suddenly anything sounds better than the task in front of you. The desert monks of Egypt knew this hour well enough to name it.

Evagrius, a monk who lived among them, called it the noonday demon, and he describes it like someone who knew it from the inside: the sun seems not to move, the day feels endless, and the monk keeps getting up to look out the window, to see if anyone is coming.

teach.b: The name echoes a psalm that promises safety from "the destruction that wasteth at noonday."

Evagrius's word for it was acedia: a heavy, restless boredom that makes your own place feel unbearable. It whispers that the work would be easier somewhere else, that this life is pointless, that you should go.
For the desert tradition this wasn't laziness to be scolded. It was one of the eight thoughts a monk had to learn to see coming. And there's a story about what to do.
Abba Antony, honored as a father of the desert monks, sat in the desert weighed down by acedia, and he prayed: Lord, I want to be saved, but these thoughts won't leave me alone.
Then he saw someone like himself, sitting at work, plaiting rope, then standing to pray, then sitting to plait again. It was an angel, and it said: do this, and you will be saved. Antony took heart.
That's the teaching: in the desert tradition, the heavy hour is met by staying put and alternating, a little work, a little prayer, not by running.
Evagrius adds that whoever waits it out finds peace and joy coming after it.
On your own path that becomes something small at three o'clock: don't flee the hour, don't fight it, breathe through it, and go back to the rope.

how: Monastic rules such as Benedict's alternate set hours of work and prayer, and some readers of the desert fathers turn to Antony's rope and angel when the heavy hour comes.

o: the drowsy feeling after a big lunch, nothing more
a short nap taken in the middle of a workday
a heavy, restless hour when your own place feels unbearable

games.q: the noonday demon: tap the pairs.
p: where the bored monk keeps looking

s: the desert monks treated the afternoon slump as plain laziness
they named it acedia, one of the eight thoughts, and learned to see it coming.
Antony's answer to acedia was to leave his place in the desert
an angel showed him: stay, work a little, pray a little, then work again.
Evagrius says peace and joy follow when the heavy hour is waited out
whoever stays through it finds joy after it.

games.q: your friend writing her thesis hits a wall every afternoon and starts planning to switch programs. by the desert story, what helps first?
o: stay with it, alternating a little work and a short pause till the hour passes.
switch programs: the boredom proves she's in the wrong place.
push straight through with no breaks until the feeling breaks.
games.why: acedia whispers that anywhere else would be better. the desert answer is Antony's angel: stay, plait, pray, plait again.

practice: Sit up and let three long sighs go, in through the nose and slowly out through the mouth, letting the shoulders drop each time. Then stand once, as Antony's angel stood from the rope to pray, and sit back down.
Let a few ordinary breaths come, staying right where you are.

wordCard.voice: The afternoon slump: the heavy hour. The desert monks called it acedia, the noonday demon, and met it by staying.

orig.note: Greek: acedia, the desert monks' word for the heavy, restless hour.

carryVoice: Your line: the heavy hour. Stay put, a little work and a little prayer, like Antony's angel with the rope. That's the afternoon, held.
